title: Hillel the Last
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: The supplied text places this Hillel in the fourteenth generation from Hillel the Babylonian, for he was the son of Rabbi Yehudah Nesia the third, son of Rabbi Gamliel, son of Rabbi Yehudah Nesia the second, son of Rabbi Gamliel, son of Rabbi Yehudah Nesia the first, son of Rabban Gamliel, son of our holy Rabbi, son of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel of Usha, son of Rabban Gamliel of Yavneh, son of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel who was executed, son of Rabban Gamliel the Elder, son of Shimon, son of Hillel the Babylonian. Hyman reports that he is not mentioned further in either the Babylonian or the Jerusalem Talmud; only his name has remained a blessing for all generations through the great enactment made by him, as cited in the Ramban, in [Sefer HaZekhut, tractate Gittin, chapter HaSholeach](https://www.sefaria.org/Sefer_HaZekhut_on_Gittin.18a.1): “From the days of Hillel son of Rabbi Yehudah Nesia, in the year 670 of the Seleucid era, 4118 [of the creation], the Sanhedrin ceased in the Land of Israel and experts ceased from it; and it was he who established the order of intercalation, counted years and sanctified months for the generations.”

Hyman likewise cites Yuchasin for a tradition in Sefer HaIbbur in the name of our master Hai Gaon; but Hyman identifies a scribal error there, saying that he was the son of Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi; he proposes Nesia.

Hyman cites R. Zechariah Frankel’s Mavo HaYerushalmi, addenda, p. 146b, as saying that among the writings of the emperor Julian there is found a letter he wrote to Hillel Nesia, full of love, peace and blessing, calling him “the brother Iulos the Patriarch,” the most honored. Hyman’s historical account continues: from the year 662 of the Seleucid era onward, Gallus, the emperor’s deputy, came to the lands of the East with his general, the wicked Ursicinus, and destroyed most of the settlements of the Land of Israel. They destroyed also the town of Tzippori, where Rabbi Chanina was (who left his crown to Rabbi Mana, son of Rabbi Yonah), as Hyman cites the beginning of Yevamot, chapter 15: “In the days of Ursicinus the people of Tzippori were sought, and they put patches over their nostrils,” as cited at length in the precious book Erekh Milin, entry Ursicinus. Nearly all the settlements of Israel were destroyed — were it not that the Lord, in His great mercy, sent His help from on high, the emperor Julian, who reigned only two years, whose heart was good toward the Jews, and who pursued the new sect in anger and wrath. Hillel Nesia saw and understood with his mind’s eye that strength does not last forever, and that in the end the priests would raise their heads as before. Then he gathered an ordained and expert court in the Land of Israel and sanctified months and intercalated years until the days of the Messiah. He needed this because, although the people of Babylonia were already expert in the fixing of the month, as in [Beitzah 4b](https://www.sefaria.org/Beitzah.4b.9-12), what use was this if they did not know how they fixed it in the Land of Israel? This was his great enactment. And so it was: this precious emperor was killed, and then his plans perished — he had thought good for the Jews, to return and rebuild the Temple — and the priests of the religion returned and renewed the decrees, and hardly any remnant of Israel was left in all the Land of Israel.

notes.text: Hyman explicitly gives 670 and 662 of the Seleucid era and 4118 for the former, without further conversion. יולאז is rendered Iulos as supplied. Genealogy, calendar-enactment chronology, Julian narrative and language about the new sect/priests are Hyman’s attributed historical account, not independently established chronology here. The supplied quotation has איספלגי on their noses; the earlier confident plasters translation is withdrawn pending a named matching passage/lexical determination. The saved Guggenheimer Jerusalem Talmud Yevamot15:1 text was read in full and does not contain the Ursicinus quotation; this bounded nonmatch does not establish its absence elsewhere or an error in printed Hyman. This quotation/word remains a source hold.

The Ursicinus story is at [Jerusalem Talmud Yevamot 16:3:2](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Yevamot.16.3.2), with a parallel in [Sotah 9:3:2](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Sotah.9.3.2). Both describe people from Tzippori using patches over their nostrils to avoid recognition and being found after someone denounced them. The broader destruction account is Hyman’s.

The supplied text says fourteenth generation (יד׳), where Hyman’s print reads thirteenth (יג׳). In Sefer HaZekhut on Gittin 18a:1, Ramban gives 670 of the Seleucid era and attributes the calendar enactment to Hillel, son of Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi. The consulted text does not include Hyman’s equivalent year 4118. The consulted Yuchasin calls its Hillel tenth from Hillel the Elder and names Abraham bar Chiyya’s Sefer HaIbbur as the source reporting a responsum of Hai Gaon. It also reads HaNasi and prints the year as חר״ע. Hyman’s proposed Nesia and his lineage are his interpretation.

[Letter 51 in W. C. Wright’s edition](https://www.tertullian.org/fathers/julian_apostate_letters_1_trans.htm#C51) addresses the Jewish community and calls the patriarch Iulus “my brother.” Wright identifies Iulus as Hillel II in a note. Hyman’s account of the letter follows his report of Frankel.
